summary: For 7-8 year olds learning to justify mathematical reasoning: help children move from checking a few examples toward arguing why a GENERAL statement must be true for all cases (the empirical-to-structural shift). Core moves: build multi-step because/therefore chains, use generic/visual proofs (an even number as pairs with none left over), disprove a universal claim with a single counter-example, and locate and explain the faulty step in a worked example grounded in place value. Accept examples as a starting point but explicitly name that examples illustrate rather than prove — treat this as a developmental milestone, not a mistake to punish.
misconceptions: Empirical proof scheme — treating a few confirming examples as proof that a general statement is always true
Convincing-not-justifying — a confident argument with missing steps, close to but not yet a complete chain
Identifying an error only as 'the answer is different' rather than naming the faulty step and why
Not realising that one counter-example is enough to disprove a general statement

activities.title: Convince the friendly skeptic
steps: State a general claim, e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number', and offer an example such as 4 + 6 = 10
Respond to a partner (an adult or a role-play) who cheerfully agrees each example is even but keeps asking: 'Can you give me another? And another?'
Face the key question: 'I believe every pair you've tried — but even numbers go on forever, so you could never check them all. How do you KNOW there isn't one pair that breaks it?'
Reach for a reason that covers all cases at once, e.g. 'every even number is made of pairs with none left over, so two of them still make complete pairs, so the total is even'
Then take a FALSE statement from the partner (e.g. 'adding two numbers always gives an even number') and topple it with a single counter-example such as 2 + 3 = 5
activities.insight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.

activities.title: Build and test an argument workspace
steps: Take a statement such as 'two evens → even' and run it against several cases, noticing that no number of green ticks ever proves it for all cases
Use a grouping tool (physical counters, drawn dots, or an on-screen manipulative) to split a number into pairs with none left over, then show that two such numbers still make complete pairs

Sort statements into always / sometimes / never true. To reject a claim that something is ALWAYS true, give one counter-example that breaks it; to reject a claim that something is NEVER true, give one case where it does hold; for a statement that is genuinely SOMETIMES true, show both a case where it holds and a case where it does not
Build the argument as a chain: 'every even number splits into pairs, SO two evens are pairs plus pairs, THEREFORE the total is even' — and check each link follows from the last
activities.insight: Testing cases can suggest a conjecture, but a generic argument built from how numbers are structured is what establishes it for every case. Always/sometimes/never sorting sharpens disproof: one counter-example rejects a claimed 'always', one confirming case rejects a claimed 'never', while a 'sometimes' claim needs a case each way.

activities.title: Spot and explain the faulty step
steps: Examine a worked columnar addition that contains a deliberate error (e.g. incorrect regrouping between the ones and tens columns)
Locate the exact step that is wrong — not just notice the final answer differs from your own
Explain WHY it is wrong in terms of place value, e.g. 'the ten that should have been carried into the tens column was dropped'
Say what should have happened in that column to make it correct
activities.insight: Finding an error means naming the specific faulty step and the place-value rule it breaks, not merely observing that the answer looks different.

checkQuestion: Ask: 'Someone says, "If you add two even numbers you always get an even number." Is that true? How do you KNOW it is true for every pair of even numbers, not just the ones you tried?' Then show a columnar addition with a regrouping error and ask: 'Find the mistake and explain why it's wrong.' Discuss the reasoning as a whole; do not score a single answer.
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for a child who is not satisfied by examples alone and reaches for a general reason (e.g. every even number splits into pairs with none left over, so two evens still make complete pairs, so the total is even), and who, on the worked example, names the specific faulty step and why it breaks (place-value regrouping). Moving beyond examples to a structural argument, and explaining a flaw, are the targets.
